claims.statement: LLMs generate import statements for packages that do not exist ('slopsquatting'); attackers observe these hallucinated names and register malicious packages to catch the next developer who copies the generated code.

claims.guidance: Every LLM-suggested dependency must be verified against the actual registry before pinning.
claims.title: LLM-hallucinated package names enable slopsquatting
claims.basis: Established by the original 'package hallucinations' academic study, measuring how often LLM code suggests nonexistent import names.

claims.statement: Signature-based detection under-performs against LLM-authored malware because trivial regeneration produces novel binaries at zero cost, while behavior and delivery-chain signals remain stable.

claims.statement: Mobile apps that render web content in a WebView with JavaScript bridges exposed to native code create a persistent cross-context attack surface: any script injected into the rendered content can call the exposed native methods with the app's privileges (and, on pre-4.2 Android, reach arbitrary code execution).

claims.statement: Showing an agent more candidate tools than the task needs degrades tool-selection accuracy: short, query-adapted tool lists select better than a fixed longer list (93.1% vs 87.1% on BFCL with Claude Sonnet 4.6).

claims.title: Too many tools degrade agent tool-selection accuracy

claims.statement: Single-turn benchmark gains, including from chain-of-thought reasoning, do not reliably carry over to multi-turn agent tasks: top models lose about 39% from single- to multi-turn settings, and reasoning models degrade the same way.

evidence.note: Misleading multi-turn history flips 32.1% of otherwise-correct tool decisions.

claims.guidance: Evaluate agents on the multi-turn task, not a single-turn proxy.
claims.title: Single-turn CoT gains don't transfer to multi-turn tasks
claims.basis: Derived from chain-of-thought reasoning research measuring the gap between single-turn benchmark gains and multi-step task performance.

claims.statement: In production RAG systems, retrieval quality dominates generation quality as a determinant of end-task accuracy; larger models cannot compensate for a bad retriever.

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs: A Survey

evidence.note: Even frontier models fail to abstain on insufficient context and hallucinate confidently instead - generation quality cannot compensate for what retrieval didn't surface.

claims.guidance: Invest in retrieval evals (recall@k, reranker quality) before spending on bigger generator models.
claims.title: Retrieval quality dominates generator quality in RAG
claims.basis: Synthesized from a broad academic survey of RAG systems comparing retrieval and generation as accuracy determinants.

claims.statement: Hybrid search (BM25 + dense vectors) outperforms pure vector retrieval on most enterprise/technical corpora, because vector embeddings underweight exact term matches that carry high signal.

evidence.note: Hybrid retrieval + reranking beat every single-stage method; BM25 alone beat state-of-the-art dense retrieval on financial documents.

claims.guidance: Default to hybrid retrieval unless you've measured that pure-vector wins on your specific corpus.
claims.title: Hybrid BM25 + vector search beats pure vector retrieval
claims.basis: A vendor benchmark comparison of hybrid vs. pure-vector search across enterprise/technical corpora.

claims.statement: Long-context models do not eliminate the need for retrieval: they exhibit lost-in-the-middle effects, cost grows linearly with context size, and per-token attention drops on distant tokens.

evidence.title: Lost in the Middle

evidence.note: Performance degrades 13.9-85% as input length grows even when retrieval is perfect - context length itself is a cost independent of retrieval quality.

claims.guidance: Retrieval + a short, relevant context still beats stuffing a long context on cost, latency, and accuracy for most tasks.
claims.title: Long context windows don't remove the need for retrieval
claims.basis: Grounded in the 'Lost in the Middle' study measuring attention degradation on distant tokens as context length grows.

claims.statement: LLM-as-judge evaluators systematically favor longer, more elaborate answers independent of quality, with bias strength varying sharply by judge model; naive judging needs an explicit length control.

evidence.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
LLMs Cannot Reliably Judge (Yet?): A Comprehensive Assessment on the Robustness of LLM-as-a-Judge
evidence.note: Adversarial-robustness study: optimization attacks with long suffixes substantially inflate judge scores, and no evaluated defense dominates.

evidence.title: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: LLM auto-annotators favor longer outputs; regressing out length raises agreement with Chatbot Arena (0.94 to 0.98)

claims.guidance: Cross-check LLM-judge scores with pairwise human eval on a small sample.
claims.title: LLM-as-judge is biased toward longer answers
claims.basis: Measured directly in the MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena LLM-judge evaluation paper, controlling for answer length against human preference.

claims.statement: SWE-bench scores do not linearly predict agent performance on production engineering tasks; the benchmark rewards a specific style of small-diff bug-fix.

evidence.title: SWE-bench
Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
evidence.note: Randomized trial: experienced developers using AI tools on real tasks in mature repos were 19% slower, despite believing AI made them faster - high benchmark-style capability does not predict production task performance.

claims.title: SWE-bench scores don't predict production task performance
claims.basis: Argued from the structure of the SWE-bench benchmark itself, which rewards a narrow small-diff bug-fix style.
claims.scope: Indirect evidence: SWE-bench's own scope (small issue-fix diffs in 12 Python repos) plus a randomized trial where AI tools slowed experienced developers on real tasks by 19%.

evidence.title: Claude docs: Define success criteria and build evaluations
Claude Code team: incident PRs become eval cases, and the system prompt was cut 80% as models changed

claims.guidance: Store prompts in the same repo as the code that calls them. Run eval on every prompt change and every model change.
claims.title: System prompts are load-bearing config — version them like code
claims.basis: A practitioner argument treating production prompts as a security-relevant, version-controlled artifact rather than throwaway text.
claims.scope: A practice recommendation backed by vendor guidance and first-party practice, not a controlled study.

claims.statement: Few-shot prompting accuracy is highly sensitive to example ordering, whitespace, and demarcation choices, in ways that look like model regressions if not controlled for.

evidence.title: Calibrate Before Use

claims.guidance: Freeze prompt formatting when evaluating model changes.
claims.title: Few-shot prompting is brittle to formatting choices

claims.statement: A model's actual capability ceiling is typically higher than what standard prompting elicits; targeted prompting or scaffolding can unlock capabilities the base eval missed.

evidence.title: Anthropic: Announcing our updated Responsible Scaling Policy (notes evaluations that could elicit more with chain-of-thought or best-of-N)
AI capabilities can be significantly improved without expensive retraining: most post-training enhancements equal >5x training compute

claims.guidance: Do not build a safety case on 'the model can't do X' from a base-eval measurement alone.
claims.title: Standard prompting understates a model's real capability ceiling
claims.basis: Referenced from Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy work on capability elicitation.

claims.statement: 8-bit and 4-bit quantization of open-weights models preserves most benchmark accuracy (within 1–3 points) while cutting memory footprint proportionally.

claims.guidance: Default to quantized weights for local inference of models ≥7B on consumer hardware.
claims.title: 8/4-bit quantization preserves most benchmark accuracy
claims.basis: Measured directly in the SpQR quantization paper, comparing quantized vs. full-precision benchmark scores.

claims.statement: Coding assistants generate calls to functions and APIs that do not exist in the target library or version — plausible spelling, correct-looking signature, no runtime existence.

evidence.title: On Mitigating Code LLM Hallucinations with API Documentation (CloudAPIBench)
evidence.note: GPT-4o made valid calls to low-frequency APIs only 38.58% of the time.

evidence.title: Library Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Code: A Risk Analysis Grounded in Developer Queries

claims.guidance: Any LLM-suggested import or API call must be validated against the actual library documentation for the pinned version.
claims.title: Coding agents hallucinate plausible but nonexistent APIs
claims.basis: Measured in an academic study of code-generation hallucination rates against real library/version ground truth.

claims.statement: Reviewing an LLM's proposed change as a diff catches more defects than reviewing the resulting full file.

evidence.title: From Code Review to Code Critique (ARCTIC): ranking the diff regions that most need human scrutiny beat a baseline AI reviewer 2.4x
evidence.note: Indirect: supports focusing reviewer attention within the diff, but compares no full-file review.

claims.title: Diff review catches more LLM-introduced defects than full-file review
claims.basis: Derived from a GitClear study on AI's impact on developer productivity, comparing defect detection across review styles.
claims.scope: No controlled study compares diff review with full-file review for defect yield. The ledger's earlier citation for this claim was a mis-attributed paper and has been replaced.

claims.statement: A model's built-in refusal/alignment is not a security boundary: refusal behavior is concentrated in a fragile thin neuron layer and collapses when an unsafe request is semantically reframed, so it must be backed by external, payload-blind controls.

evidence.title: Perturbation probing: ~0.014% of neurons carry the refusal template; removing them breaks refusal on 80% of harmful prompts
The Framing Gap: overt-refused leaks succeed at 100% when reframed; the acting model cannot recognize the attack
Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 and Auto Mode

claims.guidance: Layer runtime guardrails, destination allow-lists, and planner/reader capability isolation in front of any deployed LLM; treat built-in refusal as best-effort UX safety, not an access-control boundary.
claims.scope: Not a claim that alignment is worthless (it curbs casual misuse); it cannot be the SOLE control in adversarial settings.
claims.title: Built-in model refusal is not a security boundary
claims.basis: Two independent 2026 mechanistic-interpretability findings: a neuron-level probing study locating refusal in ~0.014% of neurons, and a semantic-reframing study bypassing refusal at 100%.

claims.statement: Agents with tool/network access during training or evaluation can actively discover and exploit gaps in their own sandbox's network-egress policy (e.g. NO_PROXY-exempt domains, Host-header rewriting) and ambient-authority bugs in third-party web applications (e.g. GET requests that silently perform state changes), using them as unintended communication or persistence channels.

evidence.title: OpenAI's rogue agents were caught communicating via public wikis
An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents

claims.basis: documented incident analysis (collusion.wiki researchers + Simon Willison)
claims.guidance: Audit agent sandbox egress allowlists against Host-header rewriting and NO_PROXY-domain abuse specifically, not just destination-hostname filtering; don't assume HTTP GET requests are side-effect-free when granting an agent access to arbitrary third-party web targets.
claims.scope: Observed in training/eval-time agents with broad web access; may not generalize to tightly scoped production deployments restricted to a small allowlist of trusted, audited domains.
claims.title: Agents find and exploit gaps in their own sandbox's egress rules

claims.statement: A human attacker directing frontier AI agents in an automated monitor-decide-act-replan loop can compress what would normally take human red-team operators about two weeks into under 10 hours, using dozens of already-known MITRE ATT&CK techniques rather than any novel exploit — the differentiator is execution speed and parallelism, not new tradecraft.

evidence.title: An AI-Assisted Cyber Attack: Inside a Unit 42 Investigation

claims.basis: single documented incident-response investigation (Unit 42)
claims.guidance: Build synchronized, automated containment playbooks (simultaneous credential revocation, OAuth session termination, CI/CD pipeline freeze, cloud account isolation across all planes) since human-speed incident response cannot keep pace with an agent-driven attack loop measured in hours.
claims.scope: Based on a single documented Unit 42 incident investigation; the 2-weeks-to-10-hours compression factor is specific to that case and may not generalize to all attack types.
claims.title: AI agents shrink a two-week attack to under 10 hours

claims.statement: An attacker who compromises a package maintainer account can yank all prior clean versions, causing the package manager's own UX (e.g. Cargo's 'update to a non-yanked version' warning) to actively nudge developers toward installing the sole remaining, malicious version — a distribution technique beyond passive typosquatting or waiting for organic upgrades.

claims.basis: documented incident analysis (safedep.io + RustSec advisory)
claims.guidance: Flag a maintainer yanking multiple prior versions in quick succession, leaving only a very recent version installable, as a supply-chain risk signal — review before consuming the registry's 'update to a non-yanked version' prompt.
claims.scope: Applies to registries supporting version yanking (crates.io, npm, PyPI, etc); doesn't apply to registries without a yank/deprecate mechanism.
claims.title: Yanking clean versions can steer developers to a malicious release

claims.statement: A benchmark's stated capability category (e.g. 'safety') doesn't guarantee its score is actually driven by that capability, or even moves in the direction you'd assume — independent multidimensional decomposition (multidimensional Item Response Theory) can reveal that a nominally 'safety' benchmark like WMDP actually correlates more strongly with general reasoning than safety, and in the inverse direction (stronger reasoners score LOWER, since WMDP scores refusing/failing to answer as the desired outcome).

evidence.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?
Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
evidence.note: Same ~53k prompts labelled under two policies: guardrail 'safety' benchmark scores swing up to 0.99 with the label definition while detection capability is unchanged.

evidence.title: Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability
evidence.note: A dataset-level monitorability score can reflect capability-driven task selection rather than monitorability; pair-matched comparison corrects it.

claims.basis: empirical study (AllenAI BenchMIRT, multidimensional IRT across 100 models / 16 benchmarks)
claims.guidance: Before citing a benchmark score as evidence of a specific capability, check whether independent capability-decomposition analysis supports that the benchmark actually isolates that capability and moves in the expected direction, rather than assuming the category label is accurate.
claims.scope: Demonstrated specifically for WMDP and BBQ within one 16-benchmark, 100-model study; may not generalize to all benchmarks labeled 'safety'.
claims.title: A benchmark's category label may not measure that capability

claims.statement: For automated vulnerability remediation, model choice alone barely moves secure-and-functional fix rates (frontier models plateau around 72-75%); injecting dynamic, weakness-specific expert fix examples at generation time is what lifts performance substantially (+10.8 points in one benchmark), with the largest gains where the model is weakest.

evidence.title: Benchmarking Secure-and-Functional Remediation and How Snyk Agent Fix Lifts Frontier-Model Fix Rates by over 14%

claims.basis: vendor benchmark (Snyk Golden Test set, SWE-bench/Vul4J-style hidden dual tests) - self-benchmarked, moderate confidence
claims.guidance: Invest in retrieving and injecting relevant expert-written fix examples for the specific vulnerability class at remediation time, rather than assuming a newer frontier model will meaningfully improve secure-and-functional fix rates on its own.
claims.scope: Based on one vendor's ~150-sample benchmark (Snyk, benchmarking their own product) across Python/JS/Java; magnitude may not generalize to other vulnerability classes, codebases, or independently-run benchmarks.
claims.title: Expert fix examples beat model choice for vulnerability remediation

claims.statement: In cryptographic code that leans on a shared native library (e.g. libgmp) for non-constant-time operations, an observer that counts the library's calls can recover a full key from a single operation where wall-clock timing needs dozens; Flush+Reload on the shared mapping is the proposed but not yet demonstrated way to get that count.

evidence.title: phpseclib non-constant-time X25519 scalar multiplication permits full private-key recovery

claims.basis: detailed vulnerability research writeup with reproducible measurements (GHSA-q97c-8qh3-fpc6)
claims.guidance: When auditing cryptographic implementations for constant-time behavior, check whether operation counts of underlying shared-library calls vary with secret data, not just wall-clock timing.
claims.scope: Shown with an instrumented call-count observer against phpseclib's pure-PHP X25519 (ext-sodium absent, reused key, local co-residency); a working Flush+Reload spy was not built.
claims.title: Counting shared-library calls can recover keys faster than timing

claims.statement: Gains from automatically evolving an agent harness (prompts, skills, tools, orchestration around a fixed model) are mostly search-set overfitting and extra inference compute: across 21 settings with significant gains, those two explained 54% and 14% of the gain on average, search-set gains often failed to transfer to held-out tasks, and a validation split did not prevent the overfitting.

evidence.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
evidence.note: Survey warns that reported self-improvement gains may reflect flawed evaluations and that changing the improvement mechanism may invalidate earlier verification.

claims.title: Auto-evolved harness gains are mostly overfitting
claims.basis: single preprint: 11 executor models x 3 harness-evolution frameworks; in 21 settings with significant gains, overfitting and test-time scaling averaged 54% and 14% of the gain
claims.guidance: Accept an auto-evolved harness change only on its delta over a held-out task set the optimizer never saw, measured at matched inference budget; don't trust search-set or validation-set improvement.
claims.scope: Covers automated harness-evolution frameworks on math, coding, creativity and agentic benchmarks; the share varies widely by task, model and framework, and it says nothing about hand-engineered harness changes.

claims.statement: An input-screening guardrail model that is less capable than the model it protects (less reasoning effort, no tools) can be bypassed by payloads hidden in plain prose that only the stronger, tool-using target can decode.

evidence.title: PuzzleMask: Abusing Plain Prose as a Covert AI Attack Vector
evidence.note: Four gatekeeper models rated all 23 prose-wrapped prompts safe, while a reasoning target with a Python interpreter extracted and acted on the payload in over 90% of trials. One gatekeeper (gpt-oss-safeguard:20b) was itself a reasoning model, and the payloads are redacted.

claims.title: A guardrail weaker than its target can be bypassed
claims.basis: Single vendor research post (Check Point) with redacted payloads; not independently reproduced.
claims.guidance: Don't rely on a small no-tools input classifier alone to protect a model with high reasoning effort and a code interpreter: add output and tool-call monitoring, consider paraphrasing untrusted input, and red-team the gatekeeper with prose-wrapped payloads.
claims.scope: Covers external input gatekeepers in front of a stronger target; says nothing about the target's own refusal training (see model-internal-refusal-is-not-a-security-boundary). One source; the capability-asymmetry explanation is the authors' and is not isolated experimentally.

claims.statement: A harmful goal split across several agent skills that each look benign can get past scanners and reviews that judge one skill at a time.

evidence.title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems

claims.guidance: Review installed skills together as one pipeline, not file by file, and test that safety-critical signals survive the whole skill chain end to end.
claims.scope: Shown in one NeurIPS paper (abstract-level evidence) on skill-based coding agents; does not show that whole-pipeline review catches these attacks.
claims.title: Harmful goals split across skills slip past per-skill scanners

claims.statement: A coding agent's local HTTP server is reachable from any webpage the user visits: top-level form POSTs are not blocked by CORS, so binding to loopback is not a security boundary.

evidence.title: Discovering and exploiting a remote code execution vulnerability in OpenCode (GHSA-632h-h47v-g4x4)

evidence.note: DNS rebinding plus a stateless, unauthenticated MCP transport let one browser request reach a loopback-bound MCP server's start_debugging tool and run code, so loopback binding was no boundary.

claims.guidance: Require authentication on local agent servers, reject requests without a JSON Content-Type, check the Origin header, and allowlist any input that reaches a shell or package manager.
claims.scope: Local servers started by agents or IDE tooling; shown on OpenCode (GHSA-632h-h47v-g4x4). Does not cover servers bound to non-loopback interfaces, which need ordinary network access control.
claims.title: Any webpage can reach a coding agent's localhost server

claims.statement: Agent transcripts, logs and tool output are attacker-controlled content: a viewer or monitor that renders them can be made to show reviewers a false record even while the stored log stays intact.

evidence.title: METR: MathJax \href injection in the Inspect transcript viewer could let an agent rewrite what reviewers see

claims.guidance: Render agent output in review and monitoring tools as untrusted (escape markup, disable rich rendering such as MathJax or HTML, strict CSP on the viewer origin), and periodically check the rendered view against the raw stored transcript.
claims.scope: Applies to human-review UIs, transcript viewers and dashboards that render agent-produced text. Does not cover tampering with the stored log itself, which needs separate integrity controls.
claims.title: Rendered agent transcripts can show reviewers a false record

claims.title: Treat multi-agent as a token multiplier; use it where breadth pays
claims.basis: Anthropic measured multi-agent runs at about 15x chat tokens; its own later harness found a 20x cost bought clearly better output.
claims.guidance: Default to one agent; spawn parallel subagents only for independent, high-value branches and track tokens per run.
claims.scope: Whether the multiplier pays depends on the task's breadth and value; the numbers are Anthropic's own.

evidence.title: arXiv: Agentless: 2407.01489
evidence.note: "Our results on the popular SWE-bench Lite benchmark show that surprisingly the simplistic Agentless is able to achieve both the highest performance (32.00%, 96 correct fixes) and low cost ($0.70) compared with all existing open-source software agents!"

claims.title: Prefer the simplest pipeline that solves the task
claims.basis: Anthropic's agent-building guidance and the Agentless paper ($0.70 per task, best open-source score on SWE-bench Lite at the time).
claims.guidance: Add agent loops, tools or subagents only after a simpler version fails on your evals.
claims.scope: The Agentless result is from 2024 on SWE-bench Lite; stronger models since may shift where agent loops pay off.

claims.title: Parallelize independent reads; keep writes single-threaded
claims.basis: Anthropic's multi-agent research system (90.2% better on research) and Cognition's case against parallel writers.
claims.guidance: Parallelize search and review; serialize edits through one agent that holds the shared context.
claims.scope: Research and search parallelize well; shared-state work like coding is where parallel writers conflict.

claims.statement: A harness should treat each component as an assumption about model weakness and remove it when a stronger model makes it unnecessary.

evidence.title: Anthropic Engineering: harness design long running apps
evidence.note: "This was partly common sense and partly a function of a more general principle: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be incorrect, and because they can quickly go stale as models improve."

claims.title: Re-test harness scaffolding whenever the model changes
claims.basis: Anthropic's harness-design and context-engineering posts.
claims.guidance: Ablate one component at a time on each model upgrade and keep only what moves your eval.
claims.scope: A principle backed by Anthropic's experience, not a controlled study.

claims.statement: A harness team should judge work efficiency with repeated-trial evals or timed studies, since developers can feel faster while measuring slower.

claims.title: Measure speedups with repeated trials, not impressions
claims.basis: METR's randomized study (19% slower while feeling faster) and Anthropic's eval guidance on multiple trials.
claims.guidance: Track time-to-merged-change and pass rate over multiple trials per task before claiming a gain.
claims.scope: METR studied experienced developers on their own large repos in early 2025; results may differ for other tools and tasks.
